You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section indicates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

It has been revealed that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Recent findings suggest that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Sources indicate that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

It has been revealed that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

Sources indicate that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

According to recent reports, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

According to recent reports, hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (254 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34751v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98--100\% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory's gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60\% of the gain on one planted family, 48\% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61\% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47\%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them.

From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (237 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.34708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

arXiv:2611.34698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Sources indicate that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

According to recent reports, while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

Sources indicate that we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Industry observers note that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Recent findings suggest that structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Industry observers note that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

According to recent reports, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Recent findings suggest that access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Industry observers note that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team declared the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Sources indicate that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Industry observers note that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Tech Report: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (233 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34646v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

arXiv:2611.34635v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.

arXiv:2611.34624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The behavior of memory systems for long-running AI assistants is governed by a harness, which consists of the code, prompts, and configurations for memory construction, maintenance, retrieval, and answer generation. However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. The code is available at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/ReMe.

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post highlights you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

According to recent reports, reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

According to recent reports, if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Industry observers note that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

According to recent reports, the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Sources indicate that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Sources indicate that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

In a recent development, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Recent findings suggest that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Recent findings suggest that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Sources indicate that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Sources indicate that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Blueprint for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

It has been revealed that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel initiative. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Recent findings suggest that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Industry observers note that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Sources indicate that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Industry observers note that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

According to recent reports, beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

According to recent reports, we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

In a recent development, below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

According to recent reports, don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

In a recent development, the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Sources indicate that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Recent findings suggest that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

Sources indicate that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sources indicate that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Enhancement: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

In a recent development, you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Industry observers note that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

Sources indicate that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot highlights the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Sources indicate that decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Industry observers note that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

Industry observers note that for a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Recent findings suggest that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

It has been revealed that one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

In a recent development, also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.

arXiv:2611.34576v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4. In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection. On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a latest backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Recent findings suggest that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

It has been revealed that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

Industry observers note that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Industry observers note that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

It has been revealed that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

In a recent development, here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

According to recent reports, parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

It has been revealed that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Sources indicate that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, consumers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34466v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to consumers' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

arXiv:2611.34440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34432v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Aviation accident narratives contain safety knowledge that is difficult to capture using structured occurrence fields alone. This study evaluates prompting-based knowledge extraction across four dimensions: concept accuracy, verbatim evidence grounding, structural compliance, and directed relation extraction. SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct was evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, fixed few-shot, and retrieval-grounded prompting using 300 National Transportation Safety Board narratives from 2000-2020, containing 3,763 reference concepts and 467 directed relations. Evaluation combined structural checks, verbatim evidence matching, expert-reviewed semantic matching, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. No prompting strategy performed best across all dimensions. Retrieval-grounded prompting achieved the highest concept micro-F1 of 32.27%, although its advantage over fixed few-shot prompting was uncertain (95% CI: -0.92 to 2.40 percentage points). One-shot prompting achieved the highest relation F1 of 6.95%, identifying directed relation extraction as the principal SmolLM2 bottleneck. Compared with fixed few-shot prompting, retrieval improved verbatim grounding (59.45% vs. 54.02%) but reduced complete structural compliance (33.3% vs. 42.7%). Verbatim matching establishes source presence rather than evidential relevance. An exploratory comparison using 35 benchmark narratives showed that Qwen3-8B achieved higher concept micro-F1 across all prompting conditions and higher relation F1 under demonstration-based prompting, reaching 51.37% and 34.62%, respectively, under one-shot prompting. The small subset limits generalization. These findings support evaluating semantic correctness, source traceability, structural reliability, and directed relation accuracy separately.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and latest Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

It has been revealed that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Recent findings suggest that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Recent findings suggest that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the significant matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Sources indicate that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Industry observers note that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The newly introduced Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel demonstrates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

It has been revealed that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Industry observers note that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Industry observers note that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

It has been revealed that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

According to recent reports, one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

In a recent development, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Recent findings suggest that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Industry observers note that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Industry observers note that bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

In a recent development, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

arXiv:2611.34400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34327v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) outperform single-agent systems, but inter-agent communication incurs substantial token overhead. While assigning a large LLM to every agent is common, it results in inefficient resource utilization, leaving the system far from the Pareto frontier. The cost of answering a query is set jointly by how many agents are recruited, the role and LLM assigned to each, and communication topology among them. Most existing routers treat cost only implicitly rather than as an explicit optimization constraint. A fixed accuracy-cost preference also cannot express how much a caller is willing to pay for a particular query. We introduce MeterRouter, a budget-aware dynamic router that incrementally synthesizes a collaboration graph by selecting each agent's role, LLM, incoming connections, and termination conditioned on the query and a per-query monetary budget. We initialize the router by imitating successful execution graphs, then jointly refine its decisions with a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) whose reward favors correct answers and penalizes spending and budget overruns. Across five benchmarks and a three-tier LLM pool, MeterRouter is (1) accurate, achieving performance comparable to the strongest MAS; (2) economical, reaching that accuracy at 82% lower cost than the strongest MAS router and extending the accuracy-cost frontier beyond the ceiling of single-agent systems; and (3) controllable, adapting its spending to the specified budget while rarely exceeding it.
