💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Recent findings suggest that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That noted, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

Sources indicate that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

It has been revealed that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

In a recent development, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (298 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33946v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action. In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again.

Recent findings suggest that AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale.

It has been revealed that cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.

In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League.

It has been revealed that AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps:.

Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges:.

Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that the AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including:.

The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect.

“When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest.

As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership.

Recent findings suggest that the answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE:.

In a recent development, transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations.

“It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills.

“This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco.

Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place).

According to recent reports, “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.”.

— Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion.

In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner:.

Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026.

It has been revealed that the finale itself demonstrated why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge.

Figure 4: Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists on stage.

In a recent development, the 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production.

The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited).

In a recent development, in the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner.

To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments.

This mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t.

Industry observers note that A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn.

The reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win.

The following diagram reveals the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern.

Figure 5: AWS AI League reference architecture.

In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions.

It has been revealed that route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget.

This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable.

The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit said to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win.

Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact highlights up in skills, culture, and recognition:.

For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on.

“Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

In this post, we showed how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers.

We look forward to seeing what your teams build.

arXiv:2611.33943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.

EGSE: Evidence-Grounded Skill Evolution for Medical Reasoning Agents

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (226 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33909v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (184 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33897v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall.
  • In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.
  • It has been revealed that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.

In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.

It has been revealed that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.

In a recent development, before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.

Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.

Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.

In a recent development, the goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.

In a recent development, with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).

Sources indicate that amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.

Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes.

Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.

Recent findings suggest that retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.

Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.

Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers.

Sources indicate that model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.

Sources indicate that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.

The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.

Industry observers note that the second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.

The third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.

It has been revealed that outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.

These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.

Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.

It has been revealed that these four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.

You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.

Sources indicate that the AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

In a recent development, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Sources indicate that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Industry observers note that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Industry observers note that figure 1. Upcoming public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

It has been revealed that publicly available genomic data has proved key in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

According to recent reports, making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Sources indicate that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Industry observers note that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Recent findings suggest that teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

It has been revealed that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be declared through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

According to recent reports, we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message. Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

arXiv:2611.33836v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release.
  • Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region.
  • Sources indicate that with this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning debuts with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices.

Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

Sources indicate that with this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details.

Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded.

A consistent brand voice across channels.

Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel.

Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and patch prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences.

Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates swiftly.

Localization with a consistent persona.

Recent findings suggest that maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language.

Accessibility and personalization.

Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice.

With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice:.

Figure 1: The voice cloning lifecycle, from recording a speaker to using the finished voice.

A cloned voice goes through four steps:.

A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted.

For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance.

Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter.

On the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page.

If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice, upgrade boto3.

For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3:.

For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo.

Sources indicate that voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice, check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions.

DescribeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name. If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again.

CreateVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice, and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a upcoming one.

Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role:.

With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ("Resource": "*") also covers every cloned voice in the account.

Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy.

Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags.

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

For the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo.

We can’t wait to hear what you build.

arXiv:2611.33822v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.

It remains competitive with the 16-solve variants of these methods while requiring 75.0-77.6% less normalized runtime. RadOncGym demonstrates the potential of LLM agents as optimization planners in downstream radiotherapy plan optimization and provides a public testbed for their systematic evaluation. According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33818v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Sign language generation (SLG) translates spoken-language text into pose sequences that convey its meaning. Recently, flow-based models with optimal transport (OT) have become a strong SLG baseline by handling the one-to-many nature of text-to-sign. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) could be applied to further strengthen the semantic alignment theoretically, its training involves conditional and unconditional training, which may contradict the pose-space OT, thus reducing the generation quality. Under the condition dropout, one noise sample can be paired with target motions exhibiting incompatible motion dynamics, interfering with the semantic guidance when the text condition is present. To address this concern, we propose Spectral Optimal Transport (SOT), which augments the pose-space cost with a spectral feature distance, reweighting the coupling toward the temporal-frequency structure of the target motions, thereby improving the performance when using CFG. The quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

Recent findings suggest that we are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

There’s no fresh resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

According to recent reports, strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself.

Recent findings suggest that you do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability.

AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment.

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:.

Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.

Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve.

Explicit configuration always takes precedence:.

When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"], Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need.

For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification:.

With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow.

Harness supports four lifecycle events:.

In a recent development, only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop.

For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness:.

The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision:.

When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent:.

Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (beforeInvocation, afterInvocation) run once for the whole invocation.

Industry observers note that you configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.

To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow.

Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself.

The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm:.

In a recent development, the CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory.

This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you.

Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY:.

Invoke your harness with a fresh session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents:.

Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator prepares the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment.

Industry observers note that with --prompt, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt, and the CLI opens an interactive chat.

The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub.

Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it.

According to recent reports, on November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required.

It has been revealed that configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or truncation configuration, or use allowedTools: ["*"], receive the upgraded managed defaults.

If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly.

Sources indicate that create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior.

We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • Industry observers note that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • It has been revealed that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

Industry observers note that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

It has been revealed that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is major: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

It has been revealed that the integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

In a recent development, model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

Recent findings suggest that transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

Industry observers note that we then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

It has been revealed that the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report reveals what this looks like on a significant model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Sources indicate that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

According to recent reports, it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a fresh model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

It has been revealed that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

In a recent development, with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

According to recent reports, so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

It has been revealed that the Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

Industry observers note that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

In a recent development, want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.
