Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing.
  • Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract.
  • Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required.

Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file.

Teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate.

According to recent reports, amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs.

Sources indicate that with Amazon Textract Insights, you define what to extract in a blueprint. A blueprint is a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description of what to find. Each field also has an inference type that determines whether the value is read verbatim from the page or inferred from the content of the document. You can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. You can also author your own blueprint for the documents specific to your business.

For a mixed packet, you add the blueprints for each document type you expect to the same project. You then submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and enable splitting. Amazon Textract Insights splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each one to the blueprint that fits it, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value.

It has been revealed that for example, suppose you receive a mortgage application as a single 26-page PDF that contains a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer’s handwritten notes. You create an Amazon Textract Insights project with the AWS public W-2, payslip, and bank statement blueprints, add a custom blueprint for loan officer notes, and enable splitting. You then submit the file from your Amazon S3 bucket with a single StartDocumentInsights call. Amazon Textract Insights splits the file into its individual documents, matches each one to its blueprint, and writes the results to your S3 bucket. Each value includes a confidence score and the page and bounding box it was drawn from.

Amazon Textract Insights returns two kinds of fields: The first are explicit fields read directly from the page. The second are inferred fields derived from the document’s content. Both return with a confidence score and with grounding that identifies the page and the coordinates the value was drawn from.

According to recent reports, because each value is traceable to its source, a reviewer or an auditor can confirm any result against the original document. You can extend automation to documents that would previously have gone to manual review, while keeping people in the process wherever judgment is required.

Sources indicate that “We evaluated Amazon Textract Insights and are excited about its potential. Our medical bills and forms are received from a wide variety of sources and often have different layouts and formats. As a result, extraction rules developed for one source do not always transfer effectively to another.

It has been revealed that with Amazon Textract Insights, we can describe the fields we need in plain language, and the service identifies and extracts the corresponding data. Each extracted value is returned with a confidence score, allowing our team to focus their review efforts only on the fields where the service has lower confidence. We are also excited to explore the document splitting capabilities, which could help automatically separate multi-document files into individual documents and further streamline our document processing workflow.”.

— Vijay Agrawal, Vice President, Information Systems, Symbeo, A CorVel Firm.

We updated Amazon Textract’s reading engine, Amazon Textract Core, improving accuracy, strengthening the handling of dense tables and handwriting, and expanding language coverage to 40 languages for the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs. All these benefits are available to Amazon Textract customers today with no changes. Your Amazon Textract APIs remain unchanged.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Textract Core is now generally available in two additional AWS Regions, Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich), bringing in-region processing to a total of 18 AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights isn’t yet available in these AWS Regions.

Amazon Textract Insights encrypts projects and blueprints at rest with AWS owned keys. To use your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, specify it in EncryptionConfiguration when you call CreateProject or CreateBlueprint.

Amazon Textract Insights reads documents from, and writes results to, the Amazon S3 buckets specified in your StartDocumentInsights request. Intermediate job data is encrypted at rest with AWS owned keys. If you specify a customer managed key in the request’s EncryptionConfiguration, Amazon Textract Insights uses it to encrypt the job’s intermediate data. All intermediate data is transient and is deleted when the job completes. Your output bucket’s default encryption applies to the results written to your bucket when the job completes. A project’s key does not apply to its jobs.

If you disable your key or remove Amazon Textract’s access to it, Amazon Textract Insights can no longer use data encrypted under it.

Amazon Textract Insights automatically selects the optimal AWS Region within your geography to process your inference requests. This maximizes available compute resources and model availability, and is designed to deliver a consistent customer experience. All data is transmitted encrypted across Amazon’s secure network. Amazon Textract Insights securely routes your inference requests to available compute resources within the geographic area where the request originated. For example, inference requests originating in the United States are processed within the United States. Amazon Textract Core APIs are unchanged and continue to process requests in the AWS Region you call. For the list of destination AWS Regions, see the Amazon Textract documentation guide.

Getting started with Amazon Textract Insights takes four steps.

Define what you need: Start from an AWS public blueprint or describe your own fields in natural language.

Create a project: Add your blueprints to it.

Submit your documents: Send a single document or a mixed packet from your Amazon S3 bucket with one API call.

Review the results: Accept values that meet your confidence threshold and route the rest for review. Tune your threshold on a representative sample of your own documents.

Industry observers note that amazon Textract Insights supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, and TIFF inputs and processes documents in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. It is priced per page rather than per token, with no minimum commitment. For current rates across Amazon Textract, see the Amazon Textract pricing page.

It has been revealed that intelligent document processing has long forced a choice between how far you can automate and how well you can audit the result. Amazon Textract Insights narrows that trade-off so your team can decide where to automate based on evidence rather than guesswork. Learn more about getting started with Amazon Textract Insights.

Visit the Amazon Textract product page.

Follow the Amazon Textract Developer Guide to author a blueprint or start with an AWS blueprint.

Register for Accelerate intelligent document processing with Amazon Textract session at re:Invent.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

Sources indicate that if your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

Industry observers note that you are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

It has been revealed that every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Industry observers note that once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

Latest Update: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (217 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

#11426. How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.
  • Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another.
  • Industry observers note that standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.

Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline.

Industry observers note that standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs.

Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live.

Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar.

“At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.”.

— Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group.

The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases.

Figure 1 demonstrates how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Recent findings suggest that the assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria.

With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline.

According to recent reports, each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them.

The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find.

The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence.

Industry observers note that for documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported.

For live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated.

Sources indicate that in this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no.

Industry observers note that every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table:.

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix.

Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix.

According to recent reports, standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model.

Industry observers note that the assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached.

Industry observers note that the pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time. Before a gate decision, reviewers confirm findings in a custom review interface with single sign-on. There they can add the use case, review the questions, amend answers with a business justification, and rewrite the output.

The assessment produces evidence against controls. It doesn’t certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations.

International standards give every use case a common baseline, but the bank’s risk committees approve use cases against its own policy. A question factory addresses this by generating extra judge questions from internal documents. Standard Bank Group’s risk team used it to turn internal policies into checks that run on every use case.

Because those checks are derived directly from policy language, a policy change becomes a test change. Every subsequent assessment applies the updated rule automatically, with minimal manual rework by the risk team.

“Most organizations treat policy as something you read. Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. When every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy revision stops being a memo and becomes a test. That fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.”.

— Sri Elaprolu, Director, Frontier AI Science & Engineering, AWS.

Sources indicate that the assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle. During a proof of concept, it is optional, giving teams an early view of potential gaps. At the build stage, it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group’s production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live. After live workloads are connected, the assessment will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes, keeping the evidence current well beyond launch. The bank’s teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow.

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation. This strengthens responsible AI governance, reduces compliance bottlenecks, and shortens the path from assessment to production.

This approach can benefit three groups involved in approving AI use cases:.

Recent findings suggest that “Adoption of AI at scale across the enterprise requires trust, both internally and with our customers. This assessment is proving key in enabling all our product teams to demonstrate that they are building enterprise-grade solutions aligned with both our own and industry best practices.”.

— Duncan Macdonald, Chief Technology Officer, Standard Bank Group.

According to recent reports, banks designed approval gates for systems that changed a few times a year. Generative AI applications change with every prompt upgrade, model version, and latest data source. As they take on more autonomous tasks, the number of decisions that need evidence keeps growing. Adding reviewers can’t keep pace with that rate of change.

Standard Bank Group’s approach points to a different operating model. When policies become tests and evidence is collected automatically, governance moves out of a checkpoint at the end of delivery and into the system itself. Every AI application in the portfolio can carry a current, auditable record of how it meets the bank’s standards, refreshed whenever its code or configuration changes. Risk teams spend their time on judgment calls and policy design, and the bank can show regulators the same evidence it uses for its own decisions.

According to recent reports, the same foundation extends further. Continuous reassessment keeps evidence aligned with a changing code base after launch. Newly introduced regulations can be encoded once as checks and applied across every use case. Aggregated scores give boards an enterprise-wide view of AI risk instead of a collection of individual reviews.

For any institution scaling AI, the question worth asking is how many of its policies have ever been tested against a running system.
